name: Hana Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Hana, and thanks for your time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Kestrel Fleet Services on the Northgate industrial estate. We service vans mostly, for two delivery firms, a plumbing company and the council. A normal day is three or four van services, brake pads, a lot of tyres, and a fault or two that the drivers describe badly. I like that it's the same models over and over, I know them inside out.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I own a small flat with my partner Tomasz, he's an electrician. We bought it two years ago, so we've got equity and still a good bit in savings. No kids. I'm not a gadget person. I don't use AI, I don't really want to, and I still write my job notes on paper before the office types them up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I'd hope, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was oversold. At work we'd probably joke about the office manager, Gail, who kept saying we'd all be using tablets by now. I wouldn't post anything, I'm not online much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pleased. My job is the same vans, the same jobs, and the fleets keep sending them. The only thing that ever worries me is losing one of the big contracts, and that's nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on exactly as I am. Keep paying down the mortgage a bit faster, maybe 200 extra a month. Maybe finally do the electric van course, since one of the delivery firms is switching some vans over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Secure. I've got a flat, savings, and Kestrel has had the council contract for nine years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned losing a contract. How likely is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It happens. The fleet garage I work at, Kestrel, lost the bakery vans last year to a cheaper garage, and that was eight vans a month gone overnight. Nobody lost their job, but overtime dried up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do the electric van course for sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Kestrel pays and it's in work time, yes. I wouldn't chase it on my own. I'd rather learn it when the vans actually turn up.

say: I'd say fair enough, AI was **oversold**.
I'd joke at work about the **tablets** we were promised, but stay offline.
think: I'd be **pleased** that the same vans keep coming in.
My only real worry is Kestrel **losing a contract**, which isn't about AI.
do: Carry on with the same **van servicing** work.
Pay an extra **200 a month** off the mortgage.
Take the **electric van** course only if Kestrel pays.
feel: **Calm** and secure, with a flat, savings and a long-held council contract.
S0.quote: The fleet garage I work at, Kestrel, lost the bakery vans last year to a cheaper garage, and that was eight vans a month gone overnight.
fieldNote: Her security rests on **routine** and a nine-year council contract.
The loss of the **bakery contract** shows her real, non-AI risk.
She learns new things only **when needed**, not ahead of time.

steps.text: Keep servicing delivery and council vans at Kestrel
Pay an extra 200 a month off the flat mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. That one's more likely, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible in some places and daft in others. I'd say you still need someone to actually change the pads. I'd keep it measured, I don't like shouting about things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry about the fleet side. The delivery firms will use AI to plan their servicing and shop around for the cheapest garage every month. Gail in the office could be replaced by a system that books everything, and then they'll want us faster and cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, but I'd save harder, maybe an extra 300 a month. I wouldn't learn the new tools unless I had to. If Kestrel started cutting hours, I'd look at the council's own depot, because public sector feels safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for this year, but it would be in the back of my head every time a new system came in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Kestrel insisted everyone used an AI diagnostic tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd use it, grumbling. I'd still check it against what I know. I've seen a computer tell me a van needs a new gearbox when it just needed a clutch cable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the council depot specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because councils move slowly. That's normally a bad thing, but here it's a good thing. My uncle has worked at the bus depot there for 22 years.

say: I'd say AI is **sensible** in some places and daft in others.
Someone still has to **change the pads**, and I'd say so calmly.
think: Fleet firms will use AI to **shop around** for the cheapest garage.
The office **booking** job could go, and then they'll want us faster.
do: Use new AI tools **only if required**.
Look at the **council depot** if Kestrel cuts hours.
feel: **Uneasy**, with the change in the back of her mind each time a system arrives.
S1.quote: I've seen a computer tell me a van needs a new gearbox when it just needed a clutch cable.
fieldNote: She sees **fleet price pressure** as the real threat, which is sharp.
Her plan B is the **council depot**, chosen because it moves slowly.
She would use AI only under **instruction**, and check it against experience.

steps.text: Put an extra 300 a month into savings
Ask her uncle about openings at the council bus depot
Keep doing van services the way she does now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. No. That's too fast for anybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to slow it down. Licences for the companies, something. I'd say it calmly, but I'd say it to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the vans are first in line. The delivery firms would plan everything with AI in 2028, and once the robots come in 2031, why would they pay Kestrel? They'd have a robot in their own yard. I'd be 31 with a trade nobody pays for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop everything extra, no holidays, no new car. Overpay the mortgage hard so it's smaller when the work goes. I'd look for the steadiest job I could find before 2031, maybe council, maybe something with no engines at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I don't like change on a normal day. This would be a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomasz?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan, and he'd say electricians are safe. My partner Tomasz thinks wiring a house is too fiddly for a robot, and I hope he's right, because one of us needs to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said something with no engines. Like what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. That's the problem. I've only ever wanted to do this.

say: I'd say the **government** must slow it down, with licences for AI firms.
I'd say it **calmly**, but to anyone who'd listen.
think: **Fleet vans** are first in line once firms plan with AI.
By **2031** fleets could keep a robot in their own yard instead of paying Kestrel.
do: Cut all **extras**, including holidays and a new car.
**Overpay** the mortgage hard before the work goes.
feel: **Frightened**, because she dislikes change even on a normal day.
S2.quote: My partner Tomasz thinks wiring a house is too fiddly for a robot, and I hope he's right, because one of us needs to be.
fieldNote: She has **no alternative** career in mind and says so honestly.
Her hope rests on her **partner's job** staying safe.
Her politics turn to **slowing things down** rather than adapting.

steps.text: Cancel this year's holiday and the planned new car
Overpay the mortgage with most of her monthly spare cash
Apply for a council fleet mechanic job before 2031
Write to her MP asking for licences on AI firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better than two. Still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to set some rules, so let's set them. Make the companies give notice and pay for training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have until about 2034 on the tools. That's seven more years of pay, and the mortgage would be a lot smaller by then. But the office side and the bookings would go in 2031, and Kestrel might not survive that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, overpay the mortgage, and move to the council depot when a job came up, maybe 2028 or 2029. I'd do whatever courses the council gave me. I wouldn't jump ahead of things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less. Like a bill you know is coming, and you've got a few years to save for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for the council rather than act now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't trust guesses. If I leave a good job at Kestrel (the fleet garage) for something that might not happen, I'm the fool, not the robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Tomasz decide about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still have them, maybe a bit later. You can't stop living because of what might happen in 2034.

say: I'd say there's time to **set rules**, so set them.
Companies should give **notice** and pay for training.
think: I'd have until about **2034** on the tools, seven more years of pay.
Bookings go in 2031, and **Kestrel** might not survive that.
do: Move to the **council depot** when a job opens around 2028.
feel: **Anxious**, but less, like a known bill with time to save.
S3.quote: If I leave a good job at Kestrel (the fleet garage) for something that might not happen, I'm the fool, not the robot.
fieldNote: She won't **act early** on a guess, which fits her caution.
The **council depot** stays her chosen safe harbour.
Family plans **slip** slightly rather than change.

steps.text: Overpay the mortgage every month until 2031
Move to the council depot when a vacancy appears
Wait a year or two longer before having children

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2039 for the robots. I'd be nearly 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's plenty of time for the government and businesses to sort out a fair way of doing it. I'd expect them to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be worried, because I'd be 40 with nothing else on my CV. Ten years sounds like a lot until you realise I'd have spent all of them doing the same thing, because that's what I'm like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on at Kestrel. Pay the mortgage off by 2036 if we can. Around 2033 I'd make myself look at something else, maybe a course at the college, even if I don't want to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, quietly. It's far off, but I know myself, and I know I'd leave it too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's honest. Why would you leave it too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I always do. I stayed in my first garage two years after I hated it, just because I knew where the tea bags were.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would get you moving sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Tomasz pushed me, probably. Or if Kestrel lost the council contract. A shove from outside works better than a plan.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** to find a fair way.
I'd **expect** government and businesses to sort it out.
think: I'd be **40** with nothing else on my CV.
I'd likely spend all ten years doing **the same thing**.
do: Aim to **pay off** the mortgage by 2036.
Force myself to look at a **college course** around 2033.
feel: Quietly **anxious**, knowing she tends to leave change too late.
S4.quote: I stayed in my first garage two years after I hated it, just because I knew where the tea bags were.
fieldNote: She stays **anxious** even with a decade, because she knows her own habits.
She needs an **outside shove** to change, like a lost contract.
Her savings help, but **inertia** is her real risk.

steps.text: Keep servicing fleet vans at Kestrel until about 2033
Pay off the flat mortgage by 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is a guarantee from the council or someone that people in trades get a job offer or proper training before the machines come in. I don't need excitement, I need someone to tell me where the next steady job is.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what the drivers think. They talk to me more than anyone. They're more scared than I am, because their vans could drive themselves.

headlineQuote: I don't need excitement, I need someone to tell me where the next steady job is.
portrait: Hana is a **27-year-old** van mechanic at a fleet servicing garage on an industrial estate.
She owns a flat with her **electrician** partner, has strong savings and never uses AI.
She likes **routine**, avoids risk and sees the council depot as her safe harbour.
She is **calm** in the hype world but alarmed when AGI comes in two years.
She admits she'd **leave change too late** even with ten years' warning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because fleet firms could drop garages and she has no other trade.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed job offer** or proper training before machines replace trades.
